config.title: Browser compatibility

intro.title: Browser compatibility
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple web application that checks if a user's browser supports a modern JavaScript feature, such as the `fetch` API. You will learn the core concept of browser compatibility, which involves detecting browser capabilities to ensure your code works across different environments. The main technologies involved are JavaScript's feature detection, conditional logic, and the Document Object Model (DOM) for displaying results. By the end, you'll understand how to write code that adapts to various browsers, making your web apps more reliable and accessible.
intro.usecase: Browser compatibility is essential when building web applications that must work consistently across different user environments. Developers encounter this daily when implementing features like interactive dashboards that need to render charts correctly in Chrome, Firefox, and Safari, or forms with modern CSS Grid layouts that must degrade gracefully in older browsers. E-commerce checkout flows, banking interfaces, and collaborative tools like Figma or Google Docs all require careful compatibility testing to ensure every user has a seamless experience regardless of their browser choice.

objectives: Implement feature detection using JavaScript to check browser support for specific APIs
Apply polyfills to add missing functionality in older browser versions
Construct a browser compatibility matrix to document supported features across target browsers
Configure build tools to automatically include polyfills based on target browser specifications
Update CSS rules with vendor prefixes to ensure consistent rendering across different browsers
Initialize fallback behaviors when modern browser features are unavailable
Manipulate DOM elements with cross-browser compatible JavaScript methods

steps.title: Import React and useState
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring React and useState into your file.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing React and a hook
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: The React library and useState hook are available for use in your component.
successCriteria: React and useState are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're importing both React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackWrong: import both React and useState from the 'react' package.

steps.title: Create the main App component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named App that returns an empty fragment for now.
steps.hint: Define a function called App that returns <> </> or <React.Fragment></React.Fragment>.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the App component here
steps.expectedOutcome: An App component is defined and returns an empty fragment.
successCriteria: The App component is defined and returns an empty fragment.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the main App component structure.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've defined a component named App that returns an empty fragment.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component isn't defined correctly. Check that you've created a function named App that returns an empty fragment.

steps.title: Initialize state for browser features
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, use the useState hook to create a state variable named 'compatibilityResults' and initialize it as an empty array.
steps.hint: Call useState with [] as the initial value, and destructure the returned array into the state variable and setter function.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: state for a list
const [items, setItems] = useState([]);
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a state variable ready to store browser compatibility check results.
successCriteria: The state variable 'compatibilityResults' is declared using useState and initialized as an empty array.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using useState with [] as the initial value and naming the variable 'compatibilityResults'.
steps.feedbackWrong: Use useState to create a state variable named 'compatibilityResults' initialized as an empty array.

steps.title: Define feature detection helper functions
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, define a helper function named 'checkLocalStorage' that tests if localStorage is available in the browser and returns a boolean.
steps.hint: You can test for localStorage by trying to access it inside a try-catch block or using a simple typeof check.
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a function that can detect whether localStorage is supported in the current browser environment.
successCriteria: The App component contains a function named 'checkLocalStorage' that returns true or false based on localStorage availability.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your function is named 'checkLocalStorage' and returns a boolean value.
steps.feedbackWrong: define a function called 'checkLocalStorage' that tests if localStorage exists and returns true or false.

steps.title: Create the checkCompatibility handler
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, define a function named checkCompatibility that will call your feature detection helpers and update the state with the results.
steps.hint: Create a function that uses the state setter to update the browser features state based on detection results.
steps.expectedOutcome: A checkCompatibility function is defined inside the App component, ready to be called to update state with feature detection results.
successCriteria: The checkCompatibility function is defined inside the App component and uses the state setter to update browser features.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you define a function named checkCompatibility inside the App component that can update state.
steps.feedbackWrong: The checkCompatibility handler function isn't defined yet. Create a function inside the App component that will handle compatibility checking.

steps.title: Add main container structure
steps.instruction: In your App component, return a div container with a heading that explains browser compatibility testing.
steps.hint: Replace the current return statement with a div containing an h1 element. Use JSX syntax.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component now returns a div container with an h1 heading about browser compatibility testing.
successCriteria: The App component returns a div element containing an h1 element with text about browser compatibility.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're returning a div with an h1 element inside it. The heading text should mention browser compatibility testing.
steps.feedbackWrong: The App component should return a div container with an h1 heading about browser compatibility testing. Check that you're using JSX syntax and have replaced the null return value.

steps.title: Add the check compatibility button
steps.instruction: Inside the return statement of your App component, add a button element with the text 'Check Browser Compatibility' and wire its onClick event to the checkCompatibility handler.
steps.hint: Use the onClick prop on the button element to call your handler function.
steps.analogousExample:
// Adding a button with an event handler
<button onClick={handleClick}>Click Me</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: A button labeled 'Check Browser Compatibility' appears in the UI that will trigger the compatibility check when clicked.
successCriteria: Button element with text 'Check Browser Compatibility' is added and onClick is wired to checkCompatibility handler.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added a button, but make sure it has the correct text and the onClick is properly connected to checkCompatibility.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button is missing or not properly configured. Check that you've added the button element with the correct text and onClick handler.

steps.title: Display compatibility results section
steps.instruction: Add a results section that conditionally renders when compatibilityResults has data. Create a <div> element that displays the compatibilityResults state value only when it contains data.
steps.hint: Use conditional rendering with a logical AND operator (&&) to show the results section only when compatibilityResults is truthy (has data).
steps.expectedOutcome: The results section will appear only after the compatibility check button is clicked and results are available.
successCriteria: Section only renders when compatibilityResults has data
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using conditional rendering with the && operator to show the results only when compatibilityResults has data.
steps.feedbackWrong: The results section should conditionally render based on whether compatibilityResults contains data. Try using the && operator to show the section only when there are results to display.

steps.title: Render individual feature results
steps.instruction: Inside the compatibility results section, map through the compatibilityResults state array to display each feature's name and status with appropriate styling.
steps.hint: Use the map method on compatibilityResults to return JSX for each feature object. Each item should show the feature name and its compatibility status.
steps.expectedOutcome: The compatibility results section now displays a list of browser features with their support status, each rendered as a separate UI element.
successCriteria: The compatibilityResults array is mapped using the map method
Each feature displays its name and compatibility status
Each mapped element has a unique key prop
The results appear inside the existing conditional results section
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're mapping through compatibilityResults and displaying both the feature name and its supported status. Also remember to add a key prop to each mapped element.
steps.feedbackWrong: The mapping isn't working as expected. Check that you're using the map method on compatibilityResults and returning JSX for each feature object with the correct property access.

steps.title: Add user agent display
steps.instruction: Add a new section above the compatibility results that displays the current browser's user agent string from navigator.userAgent.
steps.hint: You can access the user agent string using navigator.userAgent. Add this in a paragraph or div element.
steps.expectedOutcome: The app will show the browser's user agent string when compatibility results are displayed, providing context about the current browser environment.
successCriteria: A user agent display section is added above the compatibility results section, showing navigator.userAgent.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some browser information, but make sure you're displaying navigator.userAgent specifically.
steps.feedbackWrong: The user agent display section is missing or incorrect. Check that you're accessing navigator.userAgent and placing it in the correct location.
